article_text:
EXCLUSIVE: The sequel to Godzilla Minus One doesn’t bow until next month, but Takashi Yamazaki is already getting the wheels in motion for his first major studio pic, Grandgear , securing the cast to lead that movie. Sources tell Deadline that Sam Nivola and Nico Parker are set to join the pic, with Paul Giamatti in talks to board.

Yamazaki is directing from an original screenplay he penned. Bad Robot’s J.J. Abrams is producing along with Glen Zipper.

Plot is under wraps. Production is expected to start in 2027.

Related Stories

'A Statement' Review: Paul Rudd, Paul Giamatti And Superb Ensemble In Tom McCarthy's Splendid Humanist Look At Climate Change - New York Film Festival

While Giamatti was coveted for his role, the search for the two most prominent parts in the film was a thorough one and led to a round of chem tests that landed Nivola and Parker the parts.

Watch on Deadline

Nivola scored critical acclaim for his performance in this past season’s The White Lotus and was nominated for an Actor Award for Performance by an Ensemble in a Drama Series . He is upcoming in Hulu’s series Phony opposite Connie Britton. His film credits include White Noise and Maestro. He is repped by UTA, Narrative and Sloane Offer.

Parker won the Breakthrough Performance Award at Sundance for starring in Searchlight’s Suncoast opposite Woody Harrelson and Laura Linney, and was nominated for a BAFTA for Supporting Actress for her performance in HBO’s The Last of Us opposite Pedro Pascal. She plays the female lead in the live-action film How to Train Your Dragon . She is repped by WME and Curtis Brown Group.

Giamatti can be seen next in the A24 dramedy The Debut, which made its world premiere at this year’s Telluride Film Festival; his performance already is gaining attention this award season. He is repped by UTA, Kipperman Management and Sloane, Offer.

Yamazaki is a Japanese filmmaker and visual effects supervisor counted as one of Japan’s leading directors. He wrote, directed and led the visual effects team responsible for the global hit Godzilla Minus One , becoming first director since Stanley Kubrick to win an Oscar for Best Visual Effects.

His follow-up, Godzilla Minus Zero , recently premiered at the New York Film Festival.

article_text:
Filme tem estreia prevista para o dia de Natal nos EUA.

A NEON divulgou o novo trailer de “ Artificial “, filme de Luca Guadagnino em que Andrew Garfield interpreta Sam Altman, fundador da empresa OpenAI e criador do ChatGPT. Assista acima (sem legendas).

O filme narra os dias que antecederam a demissão repentina e a recondução de Altman ao cargo de CEO da OpenAI, num momento em que o destino do controle da tecnologia — peça central de uma corrida armamentista de IA — estava em jogo.

Além de Garfield, o elenco conta com Mark Rylance, Andrew Garfield, Yura Borisov, Monica Barbaro, Billie Lourd, Jason Schwartzman, Cooper Koch, Cooper Hoffman e Ike Barinholtz. Guardagnino dirige a partir do roteiro de Simon Rich.

“Artificial” tem estreia prevista para o dia de Natal nos EUA, ainda sem data brasileira.

article_text:
Sarà Monreale la Capitale italiana del libro 2027. La proclamazione è avvenuta oggi nella Sala Spadolini del Ministero della Cultura, alla presenza dei Comuni finalisti e del Ministro della Cultura Alessandro Giuli . Il progetto vincitore, Monreale Legge il Mondo , riceverà un contributo di 500mila euro dal MiC.

Alla selezione hanno partecipato 31 candidature, per un totale di 92 Comuni coinvolti anche attraverso progetti in forma aggregata. In finale, insieme a Monreale, erano arrivati Chiaromonte, Iglesias, Nuoro, Pomigliano d’Arco, l’aggregazione “Teramo e le sue valli” e Treviso.

Monreale scelta all’unanimità come Capitale del Libro 2027

La candidatura di Monreale è stata scelta all’unanimità per «L’elevata qualità progettuale, la coerenza strategica e la capacità di coniugare identità locale con apertura nazionale e internazionale». Tra gli elementi ritenuti più convincenti figurano l’attenzione all’inclusione e alle giovani generazioni, il coinvolgimento di una rete territoriale ampia, la solidità della governance e la presenza di interventi strutturali pensati per produrre effetti anche oltre l’anno del titolo.

Particolare rilievo è stato attribuito anche al tema del plurilinguismo e del dialogo tra culture, al rapporto con il patrimonio storico della città, al programma di formazione degli operatori e alle residenze creative. La strategia punta inoltre a trasformare il visitatore in un «Lettore in viaggio», mettendo in relazione attrattività culturale e ricadute sul territorio.

Come ha spiegato Adriano Monti Buzzetti , presidente della commissione, tra i criteri centrali della selezione hanno pesato la capacità di coinvolgere pubblici ampi, la continuità dei progetti oltre il 2027 e il dialogo con il sistema editoriale locale.

Il progetto Monreale Legge il Mondo

Il progetto vincitore parte dalla storia della città e dal Duomo di Monreale, luogo di incontro tra culture normanna, araba e bizantina, per fare della lettura uno strumento di coesione, accessibilità e dialogo.

Il programma prevede il rafforzamento delle biblioteche e l’estensione delle attività anche alle frazioni, con particolare attenzione alle persone con disabilità, agli anziani e alle fasce più vulnerabili. Tra le iniziative annunciate figurano 50 supporti ceramici georeferenziati con contenuti in realtà aumentata, un portale bibliotecario multilingue, l’app Leggo il Duomo , laboratori di narrazione digitale rivolti ai giovani e residenze creative all’Abbazia di San Martino delle Scale. Il Patto per la Lettura – il protocollo d’intesa promosso dal Centro per il libro e la lettura – CEPELL in base alla Legge n. 15/2020 – dovrebbe accompagnare l’intero percorso, per garantire continuità alle attività anche dopo il 2027.

Nel suo intervento Giuli ha insistito sul ruolo della lettura come strumento capace di attivare relazioni e comunità. «Il libro non basta a sé stesso», si legge nel comunicato diffuso dal Ministero della Cultura, sottolineando come le realtà candidate abbiano saputo costruire un’offerta culturale che «Parte dal libro per tornare al libro», coinvolgendo i cittadini e i territori circostanti.

Anche Massimo Osanna , Capo del Dipartimento per le attività culturali, ha richiamato il carattere trasversale del libro rispetto alle diverse aree del Ministero, dal cinema allo spettacolo dal vivo, dall’arte contemporanea alle biblioteche. Osanna ha inoltre annunciato l’intenzione di sostenere alcune delle iniziative più significative emerse dalle altre città finaliste, con l’obiettivo di costruire una rete più ampia di luoghi dedicati alla lettura.

article_text:
Climate journalist Bill McKibben and executive producer and former “ 60 Minutes ” producer David Gelber have teamed up to create “ Altadena: One Fire After Another ,” a documentary chronicling the aftermath of the 2025 Eaton Fire in Los Angeles. The film follows Altadena residents as they confront the challenges of rebuilding their homes, preserving their community and navigating the long road to recovery.

While much of the initial coverage focused on the night the fire erupted, the documentary picks up the story more than a year later.

Related Stories

Guillermo del Toro Tears Up as He Says ‘We’re Handing Down a World in Ruins’: ‘It Pains Me Deeply to See Three Generations Fail the Next’

“The fire was only the beginning of the story,” Gelber said in a statement. “We wanted to understand what happens after the television cameras leave, when families are left to rebuild not only their homes but also their lives and sense of community. Altadena’s story is deeply personal, but it’s also a window into questions communities across the country are increasingly facing.”

The film features interviews with Altadena residents sharing personal stories along with conversations with professionals on climate, economics and public policy.

“We’ve become accustomed to covering disasters as breaking news. What’s far less visible is what comes next. This film is about the months and years after a catastrophe, when the real consequences begin to unfold,” McKibben said in a statement. “I hope people take away from the documentary the fact that this is not a random tragedy in any way; rather, it’s caused by a particular set of players doing a particular thing.”

The film is produced and directed by Jonathan Scheinberg and produced and edited by Vanessa Gould. The documentary team’s credits include “60 Minutes,” “Years of Living Dangerously,” ABC News, CBS News, HBO, CNN, The New York Times and National Geographic. “Altadena: One Fire After Another” is currently in post-production, with the filmmakers currently evaluating distribution opportunities.

editorial_excerpt_zh: 2021年，数千只垂死的螃蟹被冲上约克郡海滩时，斯坦·伦尼的生计瞬间受到威胁。五年后，他带头发起反击，对抗海洋有毒污染以及企业隐瞒——那本该是2021年9月25日极其普通的一天……

article_text:
It was an otherwise typical day on 25 September 2021 when thousands of dead and dying crustaceans washed up on beaches in Yorkshire and the north-east of England. Early morning walkers and swimmers were aghast to find a sickening carpet of twitching, fitting crabs.

It would be the first but not the last die-off, which would see the disappearance of vast swathes of integral native sea life along an extended stretch of coast, including seal pups. It would also see the decimation of the local fishing industry and, with that, a way of life.

Environmentalists, fishers and ordinary local people wondered what could have possibly caused such a rare catastrophic incident. Meanwhile, hours before – completely coincidentally, the authorities said – a major dredging operation was carried out in the mouth of the River Tees, disturbing sediment where decades earlier highly toxic pollutants from heavy industry had been pumped.

The authorities, after carrying out a series of their own tests, denied there was a causal link, blaming an algae bloom and then, later, a novel pathogen. But those who live and work around the Tees estuary disagreed.

In All Rivers Spill Their Stories to the Sea, the critically acclaimed documentary film-maker Jeanie Finlay is not setting out to find out what killed the crabs and lobsters. “I can’t offer an easy answer to what happened,” she says. “There isn’t an official cause. But what I can do is show the audience what that feels like.”

To do so, Finlay followed Stan Rennie, a fisher off the Teesside coast, over four years. What emerges is not an investigation into what destroyed precious marine life along a whole coastline but a story about the people searching for those answers. And it has won critics over. Mark Kermode called the film “a life-affirming treat – funny, poignant and profound”, and it was awarded early film festival gongs at Bristol and the Mediterrane.

Rennie is, according to Tina Brown, “the next Mr Bates”, and much like the Horizon Post Office scandal , it is a story of ordinary working people whose livelihoods have been destroyed, who are doggedly trying to get to the truth amid cold, uncaring powers that be.

In fact, it was the ITV series Mr Bates vs The Post Office that helped Finlay gain the trust of the group of jaded fishers, who by then had begun to believe nothing would change and resisted having their first meeting filmed. “After that came out, they were like, yeah you can film it,” says Finlay, who plays down her own role in endearing herself to the men, none of whom had seen – or, she says, had a particular interest in seeing – her 10 previous films.

They include Seahorse (2019) , following Freddy McConnell, a transgender man who gave birth, and, the same year, a documentary following the filming of the final series of Game of Thrones, lauded by critics as better than the season it documented.

But it was important too that Finlay is a local lass, having grown up in Stockton-on-Tees. When she first came across the story, it “made me think about the coastline that I knew and loved, the place that made me”. “I didn’t have to research it because I knew them. I knew them really, really well because this is my home,” she says.

We are introduced to Rennie in the opening scenes, as he explains from his boat, “All my life’s just been about fishing.” This is palpable over a video call from his home in Teesside, as he rattles off fishing jargon, in among complex scientific explanations and legal and bureaucratic terms in a whirlwind, telling the story of the past five years of his life.

He had pulled in some lobster pots that day in 2021 to find only dead lobsters in there. “We just knew that there was something wrong. Within a couple of days, the life had disappeared totally.”

It was disturbing, he says, to speak to his friends and realise they too had seen the devastation. “I got involved from then onwards, doing everything I could to campaign to get to the truth.”

Rennie has spent decades caring profoundly about the sealife on his doorstep. He would fish a mile away from the entrance of the Tees, in what had been some of the richest lobster grounds in the UK, thanks to sustainable fishing practices. “In all my life I’ve never kept a big lobster,” he says, explaining the process of cutting a v-shaped notch in the tails of large females and returning them to the sea. V-notched lobsters are illegal to sell in parts of the UK, so this act prevents them from ever being eaten, protecting them their entire 50-year lifespans.

“We could have landed thousands of lobsters, but we thought we were doing our bit and it certainly seemed to be working. And then overnight, all of them years, you think, what have we achieved? Because everything was dead.”

He is both the natural and reluctant leader of the North East Fishing Collective (NEFC), a group made up of about 60 fishers, many of whom found themselves swamped with debt and unable to take care of their families. Rennie is joined in his quest by Dr Sue Wilson from Tara Seal Research, who watched all the seal pups born along that same coastline perish, , chemist Dr Simon Gibbon and marine biologist Dr Gary Caldwell.

“You can say it’s done,” says Finlay. “It’s not done for Stan. It’s not done for Sue. It’s not done for the scientists … or for Simon Gibbon, the chemist who’s trying to get the dredge licence put on hold.”

That is something the viewers have understood better than the authorities, as money has poured into an NEFC £100,000 fundraiser for the next round of scientific testing. “Someone in Glasgow donated £1,000 during the Q&A on the night, and people have been putting £5 in the pot, it’s pretty amazing.”

Rennie says audience members have been angry on their behalf, and some have cried. “For strangers who aren’t from the area to have that same reaction, it blows your mind.”

Finlay says: “People are becoming infuriated by elected officials who use their enormous platform, their enormous loudhailer, to tell you stories that are greatly at odds with lived experience. Our lives are dominated by tech bros and platforms and conglomerates and people that shout very loudly. And that can often feel disconnected from real life.”

On top of that, Finlay says, people are simply disgusted by the state of the UK’s waterways. “You can sell off all the utilities in the country, and now we’re living with the consequences of that. You can make as many promises as you like, you can promise as many jobs as you like. But the reality is, the trains aren’t working and there’s poo in the river and everyone’s pissed off with that.”

All Rivers Spill Their Stories to the Sea is in cinemas from 23 October.

{"type": "paragraph", "text": "乔希·加德纳（Josh Gardner），资深节目策划《九天天堂》这是一部富有冥想色彩的旅行游记，泰国作者兼导演Sompot article_text:
AFI Fest returns to Los Angeles this week, starting Thursday, October 22, with the U.S. premiere of Laika Studios’ long-awaited animated feature “Wildwood” opening the festival. The festival is an annual opportunity to catch the best from the global festival circuit — especially as Oscar campaign season readies for November.

Highlights include IndieWire favorite and Venice Silver Lion winner “Possible Love,” directed by Lee Chang-dong; Ryûsuke Hamaguchi’s Cannes prize-winning “All of a Sudden,” starring Virginie Efira and Tao Okamoto; Werner Herzog’s wily fantasy comedy “Bucking Fastard,” starring Kate Mara and Rooney Mara; Andrew Haigh’s “A Long Winter,” starring Fred Hechinger, Kit Connor, Ebon Moss-Bachrach and Caitríona Balfe; Mike Leigh’s San Sebastián Golden Shell winner “Tender Loving Care”; and the North American premiere of Céline Sciamma’s “Tutti Frutti,” which premiered earlier this year at the Centre Pompidou in Paris.

But beneath the hood of the buzzier titles are plenty of lesser-sung selections worth your time, and a ticket. Below, IndieWire polled the AFI Fest programmers for their favorite films out of the features and shorts sections to help guide your long weekend at the movies. See the festival website for ticket info and full descriptions. The festival runs through October 25.

Features

Todd Hitchcock, Director, AFI FEST “The Idiot(s)” I am an unapologetic fan of biopics and period pieces, but these genres can tend toward weighty over-seriousness. How refreshing then to see what Polish filmmakers Małgorzata Szumowska and Michał Englert have done with “The Idiot(s)”, their cheeky, spoofy take on Fyodor Dostoyevsky (Johnny Flynn) and his wife Anna’s (Aimee Lou Wood) honeymoon in Baden-Baden, when the great writer was supposed to be hard at work fulfilling a contract to write “The Idiot,” but instead wasted his time doing anything but, chiefly gambling and losing big. Englert also supervised the stunning cinematography, and one marvels at how this often silly film looks so smart. Fans of Yorgos Lanthimos’ “The Favourite” and “Poor Things” will find much to like. Abbie Algar, Director, Programming “Mouse” Contemporary masters of humane cinema Kelly O’Sullivan and Alex Thompson follow “Saint Francis” and “Ghostlight” with “Mouse,” a tender, bittersweet, and deeply truthful coming-of-age drama set in 2002 Arkansas. When shy theater kid Minnie (Katherine Mallen Kupferer, who also starred in “Ghostlight” alongside her parents) loses her charismatic best friend Callie (Chloe Coleman), she forms an unexpected bond with Callie’s mother, Helen (Sophie Okonedo). This unconventional, generation-spanning bond opens a path through grief, love and self-discovery that gives the film a wholly unexpected arc. Eschewing and subverting teen drama tropes, “Mouse” finds its emotional power in the naturalistic performances of its stellar ensemble cast, an indelible sense of time and place and a warmth and humor that affirm O’Sullivan and Thompson’s rare gift for finding hope in humanity. Screening to be followed by a conversation with director and screenwriter Kelly O’Sullivan, director and producer Alex Thompson and actors Sophie Okonedo, Katherine Mallen Kupferer and Tara Mallen.

Josh Gardner, Senior Programmer “9 Temples to Heaven” A meditative travelogue, Sompot Chidgasornpongse’s narrative feature debut finds a family making pilgrimage to nine Buddhist temples in a single day to bring good fortune to their skeptical matriarch. A revelation in the Directors’ Fortnight sidebar at the Cannes Film Festival, this simple setup uncovers existential truth about contemporary conceptions of mortality and spirituality. These ideas sparked my weary soul, fueled by both the deeply universal script and Chidgasornpongse’s formal control of his images, both mundane and surreal. A longtime collaborator of Thai auteur Apichatpong Weerasethakul, Chidgasornpongse’s narrative feature debut is Thailand’s Oscar submission for Best International Feature. Javier Chavez, Programmer “Iron Boy” “Iron Boy” is an absolutely gorgeous film; so much of the pleasure of watching it is seeing the watercolor aesthetic in motion, loosely drawn ink lines wrapped around the characters. This style gives the rural French countryside a dreamy look, as if it were a cherished memory (in fact, filmmaker Louis Clichy drew on his personal life for the film). It serves a specific yet universal tale of acceptance and finding one’s place in the world — especially for children, but adults will connect with this inspiring story, too.

Mimi Brody, Programmer “Flesh and Fuel” One of the unexpected pleasures of my festival viewing this year was Pierre Le Gall’s “Flesh and Fuel,” an unconventional romance that completely won me over. Set in the unglamorous world of European long-haul trucking, it follows two men, Étienne, a veteran French driver, and Bartosz, a Polish trucker, whose casual hookup develops into an unexpected romance. Sexually frank, funny and surprisingly tender, the film features two terrific performances by Alexis Manenti and Julian Świeżewski, whose earthy, lived-in sensuality is a refreshing departure from conventional screen romance — and idealized male leads. I found myself completely invested in these two men and their unlikely romance, which was both refreshingly unsentimental and deeply affecting. Screening to be followed by a conversation with director and screenwriter Pierre Le Gall.

Anna Li, Programmer: “At Night” Watching Beatrice Gibson’s feature debut “At Night” is a transfixing, magical experience — for 87 minutes, you wander the dimly lit Parisian streets, popping in and out of sparsely populated bars and Metro stations, observing the nocturnal conversations among a community of women. Women who are poets, academics, sex workers, intellectuals and artists, who are open and frank with each other, who muse on the texts of feminist literary figures like June Jordan and Alice Notley and in the same breath chat about their sexual insecurities. Recalling Akerman’s late-70s output, its analog ambiance and melancholy, almost Lynchian in its quiet liminality, and its languid drift in a unique autofiction form, I never wanted the night to end.

Travis Weedon, Associate Programmer “Forever Your Maternal Animal” Valentina Maurel’s tempestuous sophomore feature was the discovery of Cannes for me. I left the theater vibrating, coming down from more than just a well-placed Alice Coltrane needle drop. The three leads rightly received Best Actress honors in the Un Certain Regard section for their raw portrayal of the headstrong women at the center of an unraveling middle-class family in San José, Costa Rica. Fractured families are hardly untrodden cinematic ground, but Maurel manages a rare and transporting feat of performance, perspective and poetry, as she fleetly wends her way through the family’s knotty dynamic with lyrical direction and an empathy that never shortchanges the humanity of her characters. Screening to be followed by a conversation with director and screenwriter Valentina Maurel.

Natalia Ames, Associate Programmer “The Meltdown” Can a country undergo an authentic transformation in the name of modernity and openness, or is its forced rebranding merely a whitewash, concealing its most painful truths? “The Meltdown,” Manuela Martelli’s follow-up to “Chile ’76” and her country’s Oscar submission for Best International Feature, explores these questions about Chile in the early 1990s, in the aftermath of Pinochet’s era. The film follows a young girl (stunning newcomer Maya O’Rourke) who, much like the audience, must piece together a puzzle of scattered information, covered-up truths and blatant lies in order to make sense of a new reality.

Screening to be followed by a conversation with director and screenwriter Manuela Martelli and producer Alejandra García.

Eli Prysant, Assistant Programmer “Goodbye Cruel World” As a fan of 2014’s “Eden,” my interest was immediately piqued when I heard its lead Félix de Givry would be making his directorial debut, and “Goodbye Cruel World” did not disappoint. Capturing the magic of young love where the connection between you seems to create your own special world, Givry’s film is keenly observed and a promising sign of hopefully more films to come.

Shorts

Nichole Young, Short Film Programmer & Programming Coordinator “Chuuraa” Screens as part of Shorts Program: Documentary 2 Descend into the icy depths of the Siberian underworld in Oscar-nominated Evgenia Arbugaeva’s latest documentary, “Churraa.” Guided by Indigenous Sakha paleontologist Aisin, we traverse through the labyrinthine permafrost in search of an ancient creature. Plunge into this immersive epic, uncovering what chilling relics risk escaping the thawing ice. Arbugaeva’s haunting soundscape and claustrophobic cinematography transcend the mythological realm and natural world; illuminated by a single torch, we rediscover just how minuscule and fragile the human race is. Don’t miss this cinematic marvel that must be experienced on the big screen!

Payton Ewalt, Associate Programmer, Short Films “Trading Cards” Screens as part of Shorts Program: Animation 1 Would you steal away the innocence of your childhood for a moment of peace in your present? Visionary Radheya Jang centers the conversation of self-discovery and mental health around the media we surrounded ourselves with as children. Here, the richness of color, sound and narration coalesce into a poetic introspection that can only be described as divine. Swelling with magic and atmosphere, “Trading Cards” aims directly at the young heart and pierces through the warmth of nostalgia to haunt it with the omnipresent anxieties of the future.

Daniel Crooke, Associate Programmer, Short Films “The Bovine Comedy” Screens as part of Shorts Program: After Dark Words will fail to capture the unexpected essence which director Ratchapoom Boonbunchachoke spills into being with this follow-up work to his breakout feature debut “A Useful Ghost”(AFI Fest 2025). This is a filmmaker fully in command of where to place his camera and what to put inside of his frame, balancing a confrontational hook with a gentle human touch. The plainspoken ways he brings his futuristic setting to life are remarkable, given how unremarkable they may seem to his characters, who are simply living their ordinary lives in a world that, at first glance, may feel unordinary to the viewer. If it seems like I’m avoiding a description of the plot, it’s because I am!

article_text:
Vietnamese-American filmmaker, writer, feminist and post-colonial theorist Trinh T. Minh-ha is readying her upcoming film “ The Undying Desert .”

“I’ve just finished editing it,” she told Variety at Ji.hlava Documentary Film Festival , where she’s celebrating a retrospective.

“I’ve made films in Africa, China, Vietnam and Japan, and people would ask: ‘When are you going to make a film about the U.S.?’ They were right, because I live there.”

Related Stories

J.K. Rowling Claims Trans Activism in the 21st Century Is ‘Elitist,’ Pens Essay Defending Her Views: They ‘Haven’t Changed’ Despite ‘Death, Rape and Torture Threats’

J.K. Rowling’s Agent Slams Trans Rights Protest at ‘Harry Potter and the Cursed Child’ in London: It Put ‘Others at Risk’

She has been shooting in the Great Basin Desert for almost two decades.

“A desert is huge, majestic and beautiful. At the same time, it’s considered ‘arid’ by colonizing forces. All these prejudices about what a desert is still exist in our language. But it’s actually very lively,” she stated.

In “The Undying Desert,” she examines people’s relationship with it.

“For me, this film is closely related to the way of life of indigenous people, especially Native Americans. The other theme has to do with why we go to the desert in the first place. It wipes away every notion that allows us to conform to certain ways of life. Suddenly, you don’t have to be polite or compete with others. You go there to be with your true self.”

Not everyone is ready for that, though.

“Some just use it as a terrain for sports. They’re there, but they are not with the desert. Native Americans see the desert as layers and layers of life, but it’s even more radical. They always remember that their ancestors are with them too. Life and death go together.”

Trinh T. Minh-ha is not finished with this subject just yet – she started working on another film immediately after “The Undying Desert.” Co-directed with longtime collaborator Jean-Paul Bourdieu, it will also be set there.

“In the Great Basin Desert, there are groups of people who isolate themselves and turn this location into a research center for Mars. They plan to go there and colonize another planet,” she said.

“With every one of these trips to the desert, I could see myself changing. I was learning how I feel and what the desert actually brings me.”

With works such as “Forgetting Vietnam,” “Surname Viet Given Name Nam,” “Reassemblage” and “What About China?,” she never focuses on individual stories.

“It’s like poetry, where the ‘I’ is collective. You’re inviting people to come in,” she explained.

“I’ve always been engaged in politics, but as Jean-Luc Godard also noticed, there’s a difference between the political and politics. Everything we do can be political. This is particularly relevant for women because we’re very attuned to everyday activities. If you remain blind to that, you might make a political film about a progressive subject. But the way you treat it can be very regressive. When you turn the camera toward someone else, you also have to turn it toward yourself.”

For Trinh T. Minh-ha, “cinema is not just an experience for the eyes.”

“It’s an experience for the whole body. When I was first showing ‘Reassemblage,’ someone told me: ‘I’m hearing this film with my eyes and seeing it with my ears.’ I replied: ‘Perfect’,” she smiled.

“In East Asia, the senses are not that separate. They overlap. A painter is also a musician and a poet. I think it’s the same with film. It’s better to come with an open mind and see how it speaks to you, rather than focusing on what constitutes a ‘good documentary,’ or what its story or message is.”

That’s what she tells emerging filmmakers, too.

“You set up the rules for yourself. I’m very glad that I was able to stick with the path I chose and not be intimidated by all these oppressive regulations.”

Documentary filmmakers have more leeway today, she argued. But that doesn’t mean one should take all this freedom for granted.

“On the contrary, you have to be much more responsible because you are the one setting the rules. When people ask if your film is fiction or documentary, you have to find a way to talk to them. And say: ‘Why do you need to know?’ Of course, you don’t always succeed. Even after so many years of making films, producers or programmers are not immediately interested in my work. But I’m still building my audience.”

Artículos

Estrenos Disney Plus – 26 al 30 de octubre 2026 y todo el mes

Staff Cine PREMIERE

¿Qué verás este mes?

Conoce todas las películas y series nuevas que llegan al catálogo de Disney Plus. Cada mes, la plataforma de Disney Plus ofrece estrenos de series, películas y especiales de todas sus marcas. Conoce aquí todos los títulos nuevos. Recuerda que la plataforma también contiene un extenso catálogo. Títulos de Disney, Pixar, Marvel, Star Wars, National Geographic, Star (Searchlight Pictures, 20th Century Studios y FX) y deportes en vivo con ESPN. Los estrenos de esta semana están destacados en amarillo.

¿Cuánto vale el Disney Plus al mes?

La suscripción a Disney Plus tiene dos paquetes. Estándar por $219 pesos mensuales o $1,839 pesos anuales y Premium por $299 pesos mensuales o $2,509 pesos anuales . En ambos casos, la membresía permite crear hasta 7 perfiles, así como descargar contenido para ver sin conexión a internet. Pero hay variantes entre la calidad de video/audio y el número de dispositivos para transmitir en simultáneo.

También te podría interesar los estrenos de:

Estrenos de películas en Disney Plus (octubre 2026)

Katseye: Wild Hearts (KATSEYE: Wild Hearts, Dir.a Nadia Hallgren, 2026) (16/10/2026) Documental sobre el ascenso meteórico de Katseye, el grupo femenino de pop global nominado dos veces al Grammy en 2026. A través de imágenes inéditas, videos de sus fans (los Eyekons) y entrevistas íntimas con sus seis integrantes —Sophia, Manon, Daniela, Lara, Megan y Yoonchae—, la película recorre el camino desde el exigente proyecto Dream Academy hasta convertirse en uno de los actos emergentes más importantes del pop mundial. El estreno en Disney+ llega tras su paso por cines y el debut en el número 1 del Billboard 200 de su tercer EP, Wild. Producida por Interscope Films y Boardwalk Pictures, en colaboración con HYBE x Geffen.

Estrenos de series en Disney Plus (octubre 2026)

África: El hogar de la vida salvaje (Africa: Earth’s Wild Home) (03/10/2026)

Coven Academy: El secreto de las brujas (Coven Academy) (02/10/2026) Serie sobrenatural para jóvenes adultos ambientada en Nueva Orleans. Tres jóvenes brujas en formación están unidas por el destino para proteger su ciudad de fuerzas antiguas y peligrosas. Entre desentrañar oscuros secretos, dominar una magia volátil y enfrentarse a rivales irresistibles, también deberán navegar los primeros amores y las amistades profundas que forja la adolescencia. Creada por Tim Federle ( High School Musical: The Musical: The Series ), con Malina Pauli Weissman, Malachi Barton y Tiffani Thiessen.

África: El hogar de la vida salvaje (Africa: Earth’s Wild Home) (03/10/2026) Serie documental de siete episodios producida por BBC Studios Natural History Unit para National Geographic. Filmada durante casi cuatro años en cerca de 30 países, captura comportamientos y especies nunca antes documentados en televisión, e incluye la primera filmación de la rara pantera negra africana salvaje. Narrada y producida ejecutivamente por la actriz Wunmi Mosaku ( Sinners, Loki) . Lanzamiento de una ambiciosa franquicia multianual que documentará el planeta continente por continente.

Grey’s Anatomy – Temporada 22 (07/10/2026) Nueva temporada de la longeva serie médica creada por Shonda Rhimes, ambientada en el hospital Grey Sloan Memorial.

Temporada de amor (07/10/2026) Ambientada en una idílica isla japonesa, Temporada de amor sigue a la trabajadora agricultora Karin Shirahama mientras entrega su corazón y alma a cultivar las mejores fresas posibles. Un día, Lee Yubin, un chico de ciudad con mala suerte llega a la isla y, tras un primer encuentro hilarantemente incómodo, ambos terminan pasando mucho más tiempo juntos debido a un malentendido inesperado. Nuevo episodio por semana .

Vampirina: Una vampirina adolescente – Temporada 2 (Vampirina: Teenage Vampire) (07/10/2026) Segunda temporada de la serie live-action basada en los personajes de la serie animada original. Vampirina navega los retos de la adolescencia mientras equilibra su vida como joven vampiresa.

The Kardashians – Temporada 8 (08/10/2026) Nueva temporada del reality que sigue la vida de la familia Kardashian-Jenner.

Entre pasos: En busca de un sueño (05/10/2026)

VisionQuest (13/10/2026) Entrega final de la trilogía iniciada con WandaVision (2021) y Agatha All Along (2024). Tras ser reiniciado y escapar de quienes querían convertirlo en un arma, Visión vive escondido del mundo mientras consulta las inteligencias artificiales integradas en su programación —J.A.R.V.I.S., F.R.I.D.A.Y., E.D.I.T.H. y la siniestra presencia de Ultrón— en busca de un nuevo propósito. Su vida encubierta se interrumpe cuando se ve obligado a huir junto a Thomas Shepard, un misterioso joven que podría ser la reencarnación de su hijo. Creada por Terry Matalas (Star Trek: Picard), con Paul Bettany, James Spader y Ruaridh Mollica. Nuevo episodio por semana .

Toda la verdad – Temporada 2 (14/10/2026)

Phony: La otra madre (Phony) (20/10/2026) Misterio adolescente con tintes de comedia negra. Sonny despierta en el hospital tras un accidente automovilístico y descubre que su madre —su único padre y su mejor amigo— parece haber sido reemplazada por una impostora. Para encontrar a su verdadera madre, contrata a Sharla, una detective privada que cree en el «conocimiento alternativo». Creada y dirigida por Nick Paley ( Marcel the Shell With Shoes On ). Con Connie Britton y Sam Nivola.

Coppola, el representante – Temporada 2 (01/10/2026) Segunda temporada de la aclamada comedia argentina sobre Guillermo Coppola, el legendario representante de Diego Armando Maradona. Creación de Mariano Cohn y Gastón Duprat, con dirección de Ariel Winograd. Con Juan Minujín en el papel protagónico.

La casa de Mickey Mouse – Temporada 2 (Mickey Mouse Clubhouse+) (01/10/2026)

The Drop: Una saga de Snowfall (The Drop: A Snowfall Saga) (28/10/2026) ESTRENO EN DISNEY PLUS ESTA SEMANA Spin-off de Snowfall , la aclamada serie sobre el narcotráfico en Los Ángeles. Wanda Bell y Leon Simmons intentan reinventarse en el Los Ángeles de los años 90, donde el colapso social dejado por la epidemia del crack está gestando un nuevo fenómeno: el ascenso del rap de la Costa Oeste. Ambición, lealtad y supervivencia colisionan mientras todos arriesgan todo para construir algo duradero. Creada por Malcolm Spellman. Con Gail Bean e Isaiah John.

Yu-Gi-Oh – Temporada 5 (28/10/2026) ESTRENO EN DISNEY PLUS ESTA SEMANA Nueva temporada de la célebre serie animada basada en el manga y juego de cartas de Kazuki Takahashi.

Eventos en vivo en Disney Plus (octubre 2026)

Austin City Limits (02/10/2026 al 04/10/2026) Transmisión en vivo del icónico festival de música que se celebra anualmente en Austin, Texas, uno de los más importantes de Estados Unidos.

article_text:
Iconoclastic Palestinian filmmaker Rakan Mayasi ’s debut feature “ Yesterday the Eye Didn’t Sleep ” made a splash in this year’s Un Certain Regard in Cannes with its powerful, poetic treatment of a Bedouin community in Lebanon’s Bekaa Valley. This week it plays in a competition slot at the El Gouna Film Festival , where Variety spoke to the director.

Inspired by Mayasi’s grandmother, it’s a story of two women who become pawns in a tribal blood feud, played out in a visionary style that owes much to Mayasi’s mentor Abbas Kiarostami, yet has its own rhythm and sensorial, at times almost feverish, point of view. Following its Cannes premiere the film has been warmly received at other festivals, and will be screening at Montpellier’s CineMed followed immediately by the Rome Film Festival, in their Best First Feature section. International sales are being handled by Salaud Morisset .

The film has several exceptional set pieces: it opens with a car in flames, in the middle there’s a stunningly hallucinatory wedding sequence, and it ends with an evocative longshot that plays with visual space. When you and your cinematographer Pôl Seif were conceiving the film, did you have these already in mind?

Some of it was already set and ready in our minds. Some of it, no. For example, for sure the fire, it was there since the beginning. I’m interested in metaphors and how to translate that visually, so with Pôl we had the idea that we zoom in so you feel that the car is getting closer to you and the fire is spreading. We were trying to translate what the metaphor could possibly look like. Whereas the end was rewritten, by the two of us, because it’s a very visual scene. So we blocked it again three days before the shoot ended, and we rewrote it entirely.

The wedding scene has been singled out by many critics for its visual beauty and the emotional shift it conveys.

In that scene I allowed myself to get out of the narrative, so to speak, to change the rhythm and play with a kind of psychedelic approach. It’s never really stated that this was the actual wedding, and when the one sister, Jawahir, is revealed as a bride, it is very theatrical. The idea was kind of like zooming into her subconscious, into her imagination of a celebration. It allowed me to play around. For example, the whole scene was improvised. I never met any of these dancers before. We made a call for the biggest number of people to join, and we were very lucky because a lot of people came and they were very, very energetic. My job was to just have a microphone and make them more energetic.

The scene also allows the community to be seen in a more three-dimensional light.

The idea was to juxtapose two emotions and then make the audience feel guilty afterwards. I want to enjoy watching this pleasing, psychedelically shot dance sequence, but then afterwards I will ask myself, what the fuck did I just watch and why did I enjoy that? This was the idea.

Is that something that you enjoy in film in general? Do you like that idea of sort of thinking, what the fuck did I just watch?

Yes! My next film will be entirely like this.

Speaking of things that are unexpected, we’re used to a particular kind of Lebanese cinema that deals primarily with the Civil War and subsequent crises. Yet you’ve chosen something completely different. You’ve gone into the Bekaa Valley and focused on a community that probably hasn’t been seen before in a feature film.

I don’t like formulaic films. I don’t like the way we are seen outside, with every film having to talk about the Civil War, or the post-Civil War. I want to go to communities that have not been on film before, mainly because there’s much more depth in plots and characters and life there.

This is why I wanted to work with non-professional actors. I could have gotten actors and put them in there in this context, but I prefer not to because this fragile authenticity has to be kept. Also, don’t forget that I’m Palestinian. I lived in Lebanon 20 years, and though I don’t have Lebanese nationality, I also feel Lebanese somehow because I became a filmmaker in Lebanon. But I don’t like the mainstream, so to speak. I like to dig in and see much more into life, basically.

Is your next project also set in Lebanon?

Half of it happens in Gaza. It was supposed to be my first feature, but it’s a dark comedy, so I had to stop it when the Israeli genocide began in Palestine. Now I’m returning to it a bit slowly; it’s an absurdist, deadpan dark comedy, very different from “Yesterday the Eye Didn’t Sleep.” It’s more staged, in a more controlled environment. And it’s about life and death. and the bureaucracy of life, basically. It’s called “The Passport” and I’m in late development/early pre-production. May Odeh, who’s associate producer on “Yesterday the Eye Didn’t Sleep,” is producing that film.

What’s next for “Yesterday the Eye Didn’t Sleep”?

After Cannes, it was selected in 50 festivals, which is fantastic, and it’s doing quite well at the festival circuit. I’m doing a tour of eight festivals in October, including Rome, the Viennale, Valladolid and in Bucharest, Cristian Mungiu’s Cannes Reprise. It will also be in Geneva in early November.

article_text:
This week, Film Comment Editor Clinton Krute is in the Czech Republic, reporting on the 60th Karlovy Vary International Film Festival. Located in a picturesque spa town, the fest has long been the home of hidden gems in its Competition sections, as well as a mid-summer stop for major films making the international circuit. This year’s edition features many of both, as well as an excellent retrospective sidebar highlighting some favorites from the festival’s past, stretching back to the days when it was located in Moscow every other year.

For our third and final episode from KVIFF, Clint welcomed critics and FC Podcast veterans Robert Daniels (RogerEbert.com) and Guy Lodge ( Variety ) to discuss some of the highlights of the festival, beginning with two Bulgarian films: Kristina Grozeva and Petar Valchanov’s dark comedy Black Money for White Nights ( 04:24 ), and Martina Buchelová’s debut feature Lover, Not a Fighter ( 13:28 ) , the winner of the festival’s Proxima Competition Grand Prix award. Finally, Robert talks about Shuntaro Uchida’s drama Incinerator ( 20:49 ) and Guy and Robert dig into Hijamat ( 26:30 ), written and directed by Nader Saeivar​​ and edited by Jafar Panahi.
excerpt_original: Critics Robert Daniels and Guy Lodge join to discuss a pair of buzzed-about Bulgarian films and other highlights from the festival's last few days

article_text:
November in Paris belongs to photography. Paris Photo, the international fair installed at the Grand Palais since 1997, keeps the beat. But another fixture has claimed a place on the calendar since 2020: Photo Days, which spends the entire month gathering galleries, museums and landmark buildings around contemporary work.

“What really defines Photo Days is that we move into places that are not exhibition spaces,” says Emmanuelle de l’Ecotais, art historian, former head of the photography collection at the Musée d’Art Moderne de Paris, and the woman behind the project. The festival hands each artist a carte blanche and asks them to talk back to the walls. “We never use a space as a white cube.”

This edition, which falls on the medium’s bicentennial, has a godmother for the first time. One name came immediately: agnès b. She opened Galerie du Jour in 1986, and it has taken part in the festival from the beginning. “Everyone knows her collection. Very few people know that she is a photographer herself,” the artistic director goes on. “The photographs you see on her clothes are her own.”

For the occasion, the designer opens the doors of the Maison agnès b., at 17 rue Dieu in the 10th arrondissement, long enough to hang a group of her own photographs, taken in Moscow in 1987. The rest of the year the public does not get in. That is this festival’s particular gift, to venture into a Paris that is almost secret.

A Rotunda, a Chapel, a Corridor

The festival’s first improbable venue began with a refusal. In 2020, for its inaugural edition, Emmanuelle de l’Ecotais approached the Fondation des Artistes about the Hôtel Salomon de Rothschild. “They laughed in my face, very kindly,” she recalls. The reasoning was unanswerable. The mansion rents itself out for private events, and the proceeds keep the Maison nationale des artistes going, the nursing home the foundation maintains at Nogent-sur-Marne for aging artists.

What she was offered instead was rarer still: the Rotonde Balzac, “a sort of little jewel set down in the middle of the garden.” Commissioned around 1890 by the Baroness de Rothschild, it rises on the remains of a pavilion built by the architect Eugène Monnier for Count Mniszech, the writer’s son-in-law, whose house once stood nearby. Cross the threshold and you find an orientalist interior reassembled from Monnier’s drawings, with panels of embroidered gauze and carved wainscoting of basketry, facing dragons and serpents.

Every autumn since, an artist has had to come to terms with Balzac. The photographer Alexandra Catiere, who won this year’s Balzac & le vin commission and the Prix Niépce Gens d’images, shows “Salve” there. She takes her cue from Balzac’s Eugénie Grandet and from the Romantic ritual of contemplating the sky at an agreed hour, then photographs the evening vault herself at nine o’clock, layering analog processes to summon memory and attachment. She passes the instruction along to her visitors, who are invited to raise their glasses as readily as their eyes, and to photograph the sky in their turn, in honor of the people they love.

The festival also takes up quarters on rue de Sèvres, in the chapel of Saint-Vincent-de-Paul, the Lazarist mother house that holds the relics of its founder. Thomas Klotz, who practiced law before turning to the large-format view camera, shows “Révélation” there, the product of a year spent among that community and the one at the chapel of the Miraculous Medal on rue du Bac, kept by the Daughters of Charity, the other congregation Vincent de Paul founded. The hang runs well past the nave. “We go all the way into the refectory. You see where the sisters and the fathers live from day to day.”

At the Sorbonne, in the Galerie Soufflot of the Centre Panthéon, Catherine Balet takes over the old display cases where examination results were once posted. Outside the commissioned shows, the artistic director takes on the guest curatorship of “Humanité” at the Centre Tchèque de Paris. Inside hang some eighty silver gelatin prints by Jindřich Štreit, a self-taught Czech photographer who spent the 1990s photographing, with great tenderness, the inhabitants of overlooked regions in Bohemia and northern France.

The full program runs to 72 exhibitions and more than 230 artists, from the major institutions — the Maison Européenne de la Photographie, Le Bal, the Fondation Henri Cartier-Bresson — to some 20 partner galleries. Emmanuelle de l’Ecotais slips two favorites into the mix. The first is Elizabeth Lennard, an American photographer and filmmaker settled in Paris, who has been working over her own images since the 1970s; one of them became this year’s poster. She is showing on rue de Seine at Galerie Pixi, opened in 1990 by Serge Poliakoff’s granddaughter.

The second is Payram, “an absolutely magnificent artist,” a master printer by trade who spent his career at the legendary Picto lab. At Maubert, in the Marais, he hangs portraits of his fellow exiles, the ones who fled Iran as he did and who have been sitting for him for more than thirty years. He photographs them on a view camera loaded with Polaroid film, then prints on baryta paper, sometimes solarizing.

The program spills well past the Périphérique, out to the Maison des Arts in Créteil, where Véronique Ellena devotes “Mains d’œuvre” to apprentices at a vocational training center. All that is left is to choose where to begin. The festival, for its part, says as much at the bottom of its poster: “There’s no escaping photography.”

The 7th edition of Photo Days runs from November 2 to November 30, 2026, in Paris and the Île-de-France. Several of the exhibitions mentioned here fall outside those dates: – “5 jours à Moscou en 1987” at the Maison agnès b. (17 rue Dieu) through November 13, 2026; – “Salve” by Alexandra Catiere at the Rotonde Balzac through November 28, 2026 (by appointment); – “Mains d’œuvre” by Véronique Ellena at the Maison des Arts de Créteil through December 19, 2026; – “Que vos pas soient légers, car vous marchez sur mes rêves” (Tread softly because you tread on my dreams) by Payram at Galerie Maubert through January 9, 2027; – “Humanité” by Jindřich Štreit at the Centre Tchèque de Paris through January 16, 2027. The full program is available here .

Fatto, non detto", "url": "https://romaeuropa.net/festival-2026/faust-fatto-non-detto/"}], "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "舞台在一段被液压机械反复击打、封闭了台口（boccascena）的玻璃纸幕布中拉开。苍老、骨瘦如柴且脸色苍白的浮士德出场，身穿黑裤白衬衫。他在一种紧张、缓慢而毛骨悚然的氛围中，栖息在一间荒凉灰暗的房间里。一个金属般的声音宣读着历史上伟大思想家的名字，从孔子到康德，从达尔文到汉娜·阿伦特。但知识已不再提供答案。浮士德陷入绝望，打开了一罐燃气。随之而来的是各种出现与蜕变：一个年轻的浮士德、背上带有雏菊标志清晰可辨的玛格丽特、会书写、鼓掌并操纵身体的机器。语言简化为清单和孤立的声响，而舞台上的物质感似乎占据了上风。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.exibart.com/repository/media/2026/10/faust-castellucci.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "罗密欧·卡斯特鲁奇，《浮士德：已做，而非所说》", "credit": "Exibart", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "卡斯特鲁奇再次直面西方伟大的神话之一，质问当浮士德面对知识的匮乏时，如何用行动（Azione）取代了言辞（Verbo）。但在歌德的作品中，这种转变代表着一道彻底的断裂，而在导演的重新解读中，这种张力似乎找到了一种尚未得到解决的舞台转化。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "对蕾妮·法尔孔蒂（Renée Falconetti，德莱叶作品中的圣女贞德）的提及并非偶然，尤其是对杰日·格罗托夫斯基（Jerzy Grotowski）剧团的传奇表演者雷沙德·切斯拉克（Ryszard Cieślak）的致敬，卡斯特鲁奇表达了向其致敬的意愿。这是一种对某种戏剧的呼唤，它将剥离了舞台 artifices（人工修饰）的演员身体交托出去，以期触及一种本质的真理。但恰恰是这种渴望，似乎与该演出所特有的装置和影像的堆砌构成了矛盾。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.exibart.com/repository/media/2026/10/faust-castellucci-2.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "罗密欧·卡斯特鲁奇，《浮士德：已做，而非所说》", "credit": "Exibart", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "一种可辨识的视觉语法之原型再次回归：身体作为献祭之所，机器作为自主力量，物质取代言辞，悬置于神圣与不安之间的影像。正是这个宇宙使得卡斯特鲁奇成为当代戏剧的主角之一，但在这里却有陷入自我回旋的风险。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "各个序列不断累积，其中一些保留了无可置疑的唤醒力量，另一些则似乎更多地属于导演既有的常规手法，而非这部新作的紧迫诉求。影像非但没有开启新的意义，反而面临着退化为编码语言的风险，在其渴望惊艳的意图下显得十分可预测。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.exibart.com/repository/media/2026/10/faust-castellucci-4.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "罗密欧·卡斯特鲁奇，《浮士德：已做，而非所说》", "credit": "Exibart", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "或许，做减法正是这个《浮士德》依然需要的。在一个影像饱和的当下，激进性并不一定在于制造更多的视觉画面，而在于将生成意义所需的时间与空间还给视线。“观看并非一个无辜的行为，”卡斯特鲁奇本人曾如此提醒。但既然如此，展示亦非如此。", "translated": true}]

article_text:
Nell’epoca della sovrabbondanza delle immagini, siamo ancora sicuri che l’immagine riesca a prendere il posto del linguaggio? È una domanda che attraversa Faust. Fatto, non detto , il nuovo lavoro di Romeo Castellucci , presentato in prima italiana al Teatro Argentina nell’ambito di Romaeuropa Festival, dopo il debutto francese a Montpellier.

La scena si apre con un telo di cellophane che chiude il boccascena, che una macchina idraulica colpisce ripetutamente. Compare Faust, anziano, scheletrico e pallido, pantaloni neri e camicia bianca. Abita, in una situazione tesa, lenta e macabra, una stanza spoglia e grigia. Una voce metallica scandisce i nomi dei grandi pensatori della storia, da Confucio a Kant, da Darwin a Hannah Arendt. Ma la conoscenza non offre più risposte. Faust si dispera, apre una bombola di gas. Seguono apparizioni e metamorfosi: un giovane Faust, Margherita riconoscibile da una margherita sulla schiena, macchine che scrivono, applaudono, manipolano i corpi. Le parole si riducono a elenchi, suoni isolati, mentre la materia scenica sembra prendere il sopravvento.

Castellucci torna a confrontarsi con uno dei grandi miti occidentali, interrogando il momento in cui Faust, di fronte all’insufficienza della conoscenza, sostituisce il Verbo con l’Azione. Ma se in Goethe questo passaggio rappresenta una frattura radicale, nella rilettura del regista la tensione sembra trovare una traduzione scenica ancora irrisolta.

Non è casuale il riferimento a Renée Falconetti (la Giovanna d’Arco di Dreyer) e soprattutto a Ryszard Cieślak , leggendario interprete del Teatro di Jerzy Grotowski , al quale Castellucci dichiara di voler rendere omaggio. Un richiamo a un teatro che affidava al corpo dell’attore, spogliato degli artifici scenici, la possibilità di raggiungere una verità essenziale. Ma proprio questa aspirazione sembra entrare in contraddizione con l’accumulo di dispositivi e immagini che caratterizza lo spettacolo.

Ritornano gli archetipi di una grammatica visiva riconoscibile: il corpo come luogo di sacrificio, la macchina come forza autonoma, la materia che si sostituisce alla parola, le immagini sospese tra sacro e perturbante. Un universo che ha reso Castellucci uno dei protagonisti del teatro contemporaneo, ma che qui rischia di ripiegarsi su se stesso.

Le sequenze si accumulano, alcune conservano una forza evocativa indiscutibile, altre sembrano appartenere più al repertorio del regista che all’urgenza di questa nuova creazione. L’immagine, anziché aprire nuovi significati, rischia di ridursi a linguaggio codificato, prevedibile nella sua volontà di sorprendere.

Forse è proprio la sottrazione ciò di cui questo Faust avrebbe ancora bisogno. In un presente saturo di immagini, la radicalità non consiste necessariamente nel produrre altre visioni, ma nel restituire allo sguardo il tempo e lo spazio necessari per generare senso. “Guardare non è un atto innocente”, ha ricordato lo stesso Castellucci. Ma allora non lo è nemmeno mostrare.

title_original: My Undesirable Friends: Part II — Exile Review: An Epic Continuation of Julia Loktev’s Fearless, Endlessly Compassionate Portrait
editorial_title_zh: 我的不受欢迎的朋友：第二部 —— 流亡影评：朱莉娅·洛克特夫无畏且充满无限同情心的肖像画的史诗级延续
editorial_excerpt_zh: 注：本影评最初发表于我们2026年威尼斯电影节报道期间。该片将于10月9日在院线上映。俄罗斯对乌克兰全面战争的第1,645天，也迎来了朱莉娅·洛克特夫执导的《我的不受欢迎的朋友：第二部 —— 流亡》的世界首映，这是……
editorial_blocks_json: [{"type": "paragraph", "text": "注：本影评最初发表于我们2026年威尼斯电影节报道期间。该片将于10月9日在院线上映。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://thefilmstage.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/01/tfs-criticspick-star-orange.png", "alt": "", "caption": "", "credit": "The Film Stage", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "俄罗斯对乌克兰全面战争的第1,645天，也迎来了朱莉娅·洛克特夫执导的《我的不受欢迎的朋友：第二部 —— 流亡》的世界首映，这是《我的不受欢迎的朋友：第一部 —— 莫斯科的最后空气》（2024年）的续作。战争时期的弹性甚至比和平时期更大，尽管它只对身处其中的人开放。对于我们这些挤在放映厅里、或者如果是通过流媒体观看而驼着背对着笔记本电脑的观众来说，这个概念仍然是抽象的。相反，我们用小时和分钟来计算电影时间，这是我们唯一可以直接接触的衡量标准：《莫斯科的最后空气》时长为324分钟，而《流亡》则更长，达到355分钟。但与《我的不受欢迎的朋友》总共12小时所描绘的内容——即实时对真相的法西斯式窒息——相比，我们的观影时间究竟有多珍贵？", "links": [{"text": "My Undesirable Friends: Part I – Last Air in Moscow", "url": "https://thefilmstage.com/nyff-review-julia-loktevs-my-undesirable-friends-part-i-the-last-air-in-moscow-reveals-the-real-world-horrors-of-anti-war-russian-journalists/"}], "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "第一部电影始于2021年秋天，当时独立记者——我们的主角们——被普京政权宣布为“外国代理人”。四个月后，随着俄罗斯对乌克兰发动全面战争，他们开始逃离这个国家，这使得他们的记者工作面临判刑的惩罚。《流亡》紧接着《莫斯科的最后空气》中描绘的事件仅仅两天后开始，大约在2022年3月，为历史变得可以理解提供了我们所需要的连续性。第一部和第二部之间没有间隙，然而它们却宛如两个世界——对于我们在银幕上看到的人以及带着三年延迟观看实时展开的我们而言。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "我们所看到的是勇敢、机智的年轻女性，她们同样感到害怕、震惊，并正试图规划她们离开俄罗斯的下一步行动。然而，看到她们所有人都活得好好的，真是一种宽慰。无论你是否已经花了好几个小时陪伴安娅（安娜·涅姆泽，兼任联合导演）、莱拉（瓦莱里娅·拉特尼科娃）、克修莎（克塞尼亚·米罗诺娃）、莉娜（叶莲娜·科斯尤切科）、伊拉（伊琳娜·多利尼娜）、阿莱西亚（马罗霍夫斯卡娅）和索尼亚（格罗伊斯曼），洛克特夫在镜头背后的爱意都是显而易见的。用iPhone拍摄让她能够像在第一部中一样，保持亲近并封存所分享的亲密感，在这种情况下，保存这种亲密感感觉更加珍贵。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "当《莫斯科的最后空气》首映时，评论家们将洛克特夫从剧情片向纪录片的转型视为一种新奇事物，但对于在导演的剧情片作品中看到的同样细腻的构图以及对充满情绪的面孔的关注，却并不感到意外。一个敏捷的摄像机紧紧跟随，关注着电影中多位主角吐露的每一个字，将周围环境作为他们每一个人对莫斯科的最后印象——街道、公寓、工作场所尽收眼底。在风格上，《流亡》没有什么不同，但观看它让人感觉更加幽闭恐惧，镜头运动更具推进力且晃动，仿佛它也在试图理解那个新的流亡现实。所有曾在俄罗斯最后（也是极少数）反对派媒体之一的Rain电视台一起工作的人都已四散——有些人经由土耳其逃往欧洲，另一些人逃往格鲁吉亚——并且分裂了。现在这家媒体已经关门，是洛克特夫和她的电影将他们紧紧联系在一起。但这种团结的作用既没有被夸大，也没有被强加。这是受欢迎的，在银幕时间的每一秒都能清晰地感受到电影制作人与拍摄对象之间的信任——包括“新面孔”，如亚娜（库奇娜，莉娜的伴侣）以及乌克兰与俄罗斯记者夫妇彼得·鲁扎维奇和娜塔莉亚·古梅纽克，他们以其令人印象深刻的工作和甜美的幽默完美地融入了这群无畏的主角星座中。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "与其前作一样，《我的不受欢迎的朋友：第二部 —— 流亡》通过记录其人民的生活片段、反思以及对威尼斯（原文如此：此处指威权）国家的抗争，展现了正在创造中的历史，同时也超越了你常规的观察性纪录片的期望。洛克特夫曾将这种方法描述为“汤里的苍蝇”而非“墙上的苍蝇”，但通过与她的主角们待在一起，她将对该类型至关重要的关怀行为延伸到了任何拍摄时空之外。她将她的关怀转化为作为见证者的观众，积极地用自己的声音与主角对话，或者更谨慎地只是陪伴在那里。与他们不同的是，洛克特夫或许可以自由旅行，但这种不对称并没有让她的存在不那么令人安心——拍摄，作为一种行为和一个过程，似乎成了所有人唯一的稳定之源。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "《流亡》还使历史与现在时态以及时间的普遍关系具象化。尽管影片在幕间字幕中提供了清晰的时间戳和背景信息，但它无意中将观众置于一种不和谐的状态中。不是认知上的不和谐，而是时间上的——并进而延伸到记忆上的——不和谐，即现在即过去，却又依然存在。虽然影片存在某种按时间顺序叙述的叙事，从2022年3月推进到2026年初，但情感时间线绝非线性的。洛克特夫的剪辑用一个黑色画幅和包含地点、时间和主角的幕间字幕来夹叙夹议每一个场景，然而创伤和抵抗的马赛克却挑战了线性时间感。我们作为观众，得以再次经历关于布查、伊尔平、马里乌波尔的第一批新闻、万人坑以及俄罗斯军队施暴的记述——所有这些都被自那以后犯下的无数战争暴行挤压在我们的记忆中。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "当茱莉亚·洛克特夫跟随流亡中的主角们前往土耳其、格鲁吉亚、拉脱维亚、捷克、波兰和美国时，在任何其他电影中本可成为家园与地点的纪事，在此处却化作了一幅悲伤与流离失所的地图。《流亡》带有和主角们的集体责任一般苦涩的味道，他们强烈地感到自己负有责任（“我们纵容了这一切”是几个人说出的话），这与今天作为俄罗斯人的矛盾心理相冲突。尽管如此，他们坚定的信念依然是《不受欢迎的朋友》的驱动力，那是永不忘记历史正在此时此地被书写的冲动。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "《不受欢迎的朋友：第二部——流亡》在2026年威尼斯电影节上首映，并于10月9日上映。", "translated": true}]

The film opens in theaters on October 9."}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://thefilmstage.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/01/tfs-criticspick-star-orange.png", "alt": "", "caption": "", "credit": "The Film Stage"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Day 1,645 of Russia’s full-scale war in Ukraine also brings us the world premiere of Julia Loktev’s My Undesirable Friends: Part II – Exile, the follow-up to My Undesirable Friends: Part I – Last Air in Moscow (2024). War time is even more elastic than peace time, even though it’s only accessible to those living through it. article_text:
Note: This review was originally published as part of our 2026 Venice coverage. The film opens in theaters on October 9.

Day 1,645 of Russia’s full-scale war in Ukraine also brings us the world premiere of Julia Loktev’s My Undesirable Friends: Part II – Exile, the follow-up to My Undesirable Friends: Part I – Last Air in Moscow (2024). War time is even more elastic than peace time, even though it’s only accessible to those living through it. For us, viewers huddled in the screening rooms or hunched over the laptops if we’re streaming, this concept remains abstract. Instead we count film time in hours and minutes, the only measure we can access directly: Last Air in Moscow clocked in at 324 minutes, and Exile is longer at 355. But how precious is our viewing time, really, in comparison to what the total 12 hours of My Undesirable Friends depicts, the fascistic suffocation of truth in real time?

The first film began in autumn 2021, when independent journalists—our protagonists—were being declared “foreign agents” by Putin’s regime. In four months’ time they were fleeing the country as Russia started a full-scale war in Ukraine, making their journalistic work punishable with jail time. Exile starts only two days after the events depicted in Last Air in Moscow, circa March 2022, providing the continuity we need for history to make sense. There is no gap between Parts I and II, yet they are worlds apart—for those we see onscreen and us watching real time unfold with a three-year delay.

What we’re seeing are brave, resourceful young women who are no less scared, shocked, and trying to plan their next move out of Russia. However, it’s a relief to see all of them alive and well. Regardless of whether or not you’ve already spent hours with Anya (Anna Nemzer, credited as co-director), Lera (Valeria Ratnikova), Ksyusha (Ksenia Mironova), Lena (Elena Kostyucheko), Ira (Irina Dolinina), Alesya (Marokhovskaya), and Sonya (Groysman), Loktev’s affection is palpable from behind the camera. Shooting on an iPhone allows her, like in Part I , to stay close and bottle the intimacy shared, which in this case it feels even more precious to preserve.

When Last Air in Moscow premiered, critics remarked on Loktev’s transition from fiction to documentary as a novelty, yet were somewhat unsurprised to find the same delicate framing and attention to faces, flushed with emotion, one sees in the director’s works of fiction. A nimble camera staying close by, attending to every word each of the film’s multiple protagonists utters, taking in the surroundings as the final glimpses of Moscow for each and every one of them—streets, apartments, workplaces. Stylistically, Exile is no different, but watching it feels more claustrophobic, the camerawork more propulsive and shaky, as if it too is trying to make sense of that new, exilic reality. All those who worked together at TV Rain as one of the last (and very few) oppositional media in Russia have scattered—some fled to Europe via Turkey, others to Georgia—and splintered. Now that the media has shut down, it’s Loktev and her film keeping them close. But that uniting role is neither overstated nor forced. It’s welcome, and the trust between filmmaker and subjects is clearly felt in every second of screen time—including the “new faces” like Yana (Kuchina, partner of Lena) and the Ukrainian-Russian journalist couple Peter Ruzavin and Nataliya Gumenyuk, who also fit right in the constellation of fearless protagonists with their impressive work and sweet humor.

Like its predecessor, My Undesirable Friends: Part II — Exile shows history in the making by documenting fragments of its peoples’ lives, reflections, and struggles against the authoritarian state, but also exceeds the expectations of your regular observational documentary. Loktev has described the approach as a “fly in the soup” more than “fly on the wall,” but by staying with her protagonists, she extends the act of care so crucial for the genre beyond any time and space of shooting. She translates her care to the audience as one of bearing witness, actively with her own voice in dialogue with a protagonist, or more discreetly by just being there. Unlike them, Loktev may be free to travel, but that asymmetry doesn’t make her presence any less reassuring—filming, as an act and a process, becomes the only source of stability for all, it seems.

Exile also crystallizes history’s relationship to the present tense and time in general. Despite offering clear timestamps and contextual information in the inter-titles, the film inadvertently places viewers in a state of dissonance. Not a cognitive one, but temporal—and by extension, mnemonic—dissonance where the present is past, yet still present. While there is a chronological narrative of sorts, moving from March 2022 to early 2026, the emotional timeline is anything but linear. Loktev’s editing bookends every scene with a black frame and inter-titles containing a place, time, and protagonist, yet the mosaic of trauma and resistance defies the sense of linear time. We, as viewers, get to experience again the first news of Bucha, Irpin, and Mariupol, mass graves, and accounts of torture by the Russian army—all squashed in our memory by the innumerable atrocities of war committed ever since.

As Julia Loktev follows her protagonists in exile to Turkey, Georgia, Latvia, the Czech Republic, Poland, and the United States, what in any other film could be a chronicle of homes and places becomes a cartography of grief and displacement. Exile tastes as bitter as the collective responsibility of its protagonists, whose acute sense of accountability (“we let this happen” are words uttered by several people) clashes with the ambivalence of being Russian today. Still, the strength of their convictions is the driving force behind My Undesirable Friends , the urge to never forget that history is made here and now.

My Undesirable Friends: Part II — Exile premiered at the 2026 Venice Film Festival and opens on October 9.

"text": "19世紀後半から20世紀初頭のヨーロッパにおける抽象芸術の発展は、スピリチュアルな思想と密接に結びついていた。この点について深く掘り下げたのが、1986年に ロサンゼルス・カウンティ美術館 で開催された画期的な展覧会『The Spiritual in Art: Abstract Painting 1890-1985（芸術における精神性：抽象絵画 1890-1985）』だ。そして同様のテーマは、今もさまざまな展覧会で取り上げられている。", "links": [{"text": "ロサンゼルス・カウンティ美術館", "url": "https://artnewsjapan.com/tag/losangelescountymuseumofart"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "たとえば、 スウェーデン 人アーティストの ヒルマ・アフ・クリント を抽象芸術の先駆者として位置づけ、記録破りの来場者を集めた グッゲンハイム美術館 の2018年の展覧会や、現在 ホイットニー美術館 で開催中のミニー・エヴァンス回顧展（2027年1月10日まで）、さらにヒギーがキュレーションを手がけ、 イギリス のターナー・コンテンポラリーで来年2月に開幕する「 Natural Magic: Women, Art, "text": "この記事では、過去2世紀に異世界との交信を試み、その体験を芸術作品として記録した9人の女性アーティストに焦点を当てる。ヒギーはそれらの作家についてこう書いている。"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "「彼女たちは確かに本質的な何かを理解していた。私たち1人ひとりが自らの存在に意味を見出す方法は、決して単純なものではないということを」"},
